job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
I've grouped these by section with continuous numbering. The statute citations (DSHMRA, 1 U.S.C. 109, 18 U.S.C. 3571) are from memory and should be verified, ideally by CRS or counsel, before anything runs.

## Sec. 2: Definitions

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A), per-vessel threshold.** The 10,000-ton trigger applies to "a single vessel," with no aggregation by operator, affiliate, or project. A company can run several vessels, each under the threshold, and none of them is engaged in "commercial deep seabed mining."

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A) and 5(a), annual measurement.** The text doesn't say how the "per year" tonnage is measured: calendar or rolling year, wet or dry weight, at the seabed, on deck, or at offload. A violation may only be knowable after the fact, which makes "each day on which the violation occurs" in 5(a) hard to apply and willfulness hard to prove.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "recovery" and "seabed."** Neither term is defined. It's unclear whether recovery includes collection without lifting, at-sea processing, or transshipment, whether "seabed" includes the subsoil, and whether non-vessel methods (platforms, pipelines, tethered systems) count, given the "by a single vessel" language.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "other mineral resources."** The phrase is undefined. It's uncertain whether it covers sulfides, cobalt crusts, sand, gravel, phosphates, or hydrocarbons, so it could be read too narrowly (a loophole) or too broadly (a challenge from unintended targets).

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A), the 200-meter depth line.** "Deep" seabed is defined as anything below 200 meters, which reaches continental shelf and slope areas, including U.S. waters, and leaves shallower mining uncovered. It doesn't say where depth is measured (vessel position or collector location), and it likely overlaps other regimes such as OCSLA.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(B), undefined "Secretary."** The bill never says which Secretary. Sec. 6 names the Secretary of State specifically, which makes the unqualified usage here more ambiguous, not less.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(B), discretionary trigger.** "Risks … comparable to" is a vague standard with no procedure, notice, publication requirement, or judicial review. Because violating Sec. 3 carries criminal penalties, this invites vagueness, fair-notice, and nondelegation challenges. It also doesn't say whether a determination can reach conduct that began before it was made.

8. **Sec. 2(2), "U.S. person."** The definition covers only individual citizens and "a corporation organized under the laws of a State." That leaves out LLCs, partnerships, and trusts (depending on state law), D.C. and territorial entities, federally chartered entities, permanent residents, and foreign subsidiaries of U.S. parents. There is no ownership or control test.

9. **Sec. 2(3), "covered vessel."** The 5,000 gross ton floor means smaller vessels, which could still exceed 10,000 tons a year, are outside the registry even though the prohibition has no size limit. "Equipped for the recovery" is vague (removable or retrofitted gear), and "operator" is never defined (owner, charterer, contractor?).

10. **Sec. 2 generally, terminology.** "Mineral resources," "seabed mineral resources," "recovery," and "mining" are used interchangeably but inconsistently. "Deep seabed" appears in the title and defined term without its own definition.

## Sec. 3: Prohibition

11. **Sec. 3(a), territorial reach.** "Person" and "in the United States" are undefined, so it's unclear whether the territorial sea, EEZ, extended continental shelf, or ports are covered. Foreign persons on foreign vessels abroad are not reached at all.

12. **Sec. 3(a), conduct limited to mining itself.** There is no prohibition on importing, processing, selling, or financing seabed minerals, and none on aiding and abetting, attempt, or conspiracy. Minerals mined abroad could be processed or sold in the U.S., and U.S. financiers would face no liability.

13. **Sec. 3(a), only "commercial" mining.** Sub-threshold test mining and pilot operations are lawful, with no cap, permit, or reporting. Companies can operate right below the line indefinitely.

14. **Sec. 3 generally, relationship to existing law.** The bill has no repeal, amendment, supersession, or savings language regarding the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq.), under which NOAA issues exploration licenses and commercial recovery permits, or regarding OCSLA. A permit holder could argue existing authority still governs, and pending applications are not addressed.

15. **Sec. 3(b), scope of the grandfather clause.** It exempts "mining conducted under" any pre-enactment exploration license, with no limit on tonnage, area, vessel count, or duration. An exploration license ordinarily doesn't authorize commercial recovery, so the text effectively upgrades such licenses, and that may be unintended.

16. **Sec. 3(b), issuer unspecified.** "An exploration license" doesn't say who issued it. A license from a foreign government or an international body held by a U.S. person could qualify, which may be far broader than intended.

17. **Sec. 3(b), license changes.** Nothing freezes license terms or bars amendment, expansion, renewal, or transfer to another entity. Nothing ends the exemption if the license lapses, is revoked, or is violated, and nothing prevents a rush to obtain licenses before enactment.

18. **Sec. 3(b), pending applicants.** Applicants with licenses or permits pending but not yet issued get no protection. That gap invites takings and due process claims and lobbying for amendment.

19. **Sec. 3(c), environmental assessment exemption.** It turns on the activity's subjective "purpose," with no limit on volume, duration, or area, no approval or oversight, and no bar on selling or processing the recovered material. "Environmental assessment" is undefined, and the operator can claim the exemption after the fact, so mixed-purpose operations would be hard to challenge.

## Sec. 4: Registry

20. **Sec. 4 and 5, no enforcement for registry duties.** The penalties in Sec. 5 apply only to violations of Sec. 3, so failing to register, failing to report, or filing a false report carries no stated consequence. False statements to an agency might be reachable under 18 U.S.C. 1001, but the certification isn't specified as made under penalty of perjury.

21. **Sec. 4, no deadlines, content, or verification.** The bill sets no registration deadline, no required report contents (tonnage, location, depth, dates, disposition of material), no rulemaking authority, no recordkeeping, and no inspection or audit power. NOAA couldn't test the 10,000-ton threshold or verify exemption claims.

22. **Sec. 4, exemption claims.** Operators needn't disclose whether they operate under Sec. 3(b) or 3(c), so the registry can't separate exempt from non-exempt activity.

23. **Sec. 4, jurisdiction.** "The operator of each covered vessel" literally reaches every qualifying vessel worldwide, regardless of flag or nationality. That invites extraterritoriality challenges and leaves enforcement against foreign operators unclear.

24. **Sec. 4, resources and confidentiality.** The bill gives NOAA new duties with no authorization of appropriations. It also says nothing on public access or FOIA treatment of proprietary report data.

## Sec. 5: Penalties

25. **Sec. 5(a) and Sec. 8, timing conflict.** Civil penalties attach to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but Sec. 3 doesn't take effect until 180 days later. Courts or defendants could read that as ambiguous, and applying penalties to conduct before Sec. 3 is in force raises fair-notice and retroactivity problems.

26. **Sec. 5(a), no enforcement machinery.** No agency is designated to assess penalties or sue. There is no investigative or subpoena authority, no administrative process or judicial review, no injunctive relief, no vessel seizure or forfeiture, no citizen suit, and no penalty factors.

27. **Sec. 5(b), mens rea.** "Willfully" is undefined, and combined with the vague terms in Sec. 2 it gives defendants a strong good-faith defense. Organizational fines default to 18 U.S.C. 3571, generally capped at $500,000 per felony count unless the gain/loss alternative applies, which could be lower than the civil maximum.

28. **Sec. 5, who is liable.** "Any person who violates" doesn't address parent companies, financiers, charterers, or officers directing the conduct. Corporate structuring can therefore shield the real decision-makers.

## Secs. 6–8: International agreement, duration, effective date

29. **Sec. 6, international agreement.** "Shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months" is ambiguous about whether the deadline is for starting or concluding talks, and "seek" makes it non-binding. There is no reporting requirement or consequence, "equivalent" is undefined, the form of agreement (treaty or executive agreement) is unspecified, and the clock runs from enactment, not the effective date.

30. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b), internal conflict.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition lasts until Congress finds otherwise, but (b) ends the entire Act after 10 years regardless. Subsection (a) is therefore largely illusory, and with Sec. 8 the prohibition operates for about 9.5 years.

31. **Sec. 7(a), mechanics.** The bill doesn't require the National Academies report, set a deadline or funding for it, or define "serious harm." It provides no expedited procedure for the joint resolution (which is subject to veto) and doesn't say whether a finding automatically lifts the prohibition. Congress could also repeal by ordinary legislation anyway.

32. **Sec. 7(b), no savings clause.** The bill doesn't say whether violations committed before the sunset can still be prosecuted or penalized afterward. The general savings statute (1 U.S.C. 109) addresses repeals, and whether it covers self-expiring statutes is uncertain.

33. **Sec. 8, 180-day gap.** Companies can ramp up operations, sign contracts, and build reliance interests (supporting vested-rights or takings arguments) before the prohibition applies. The bill uses two different clocks, enactment for Secs. 3(b), 5(a), 6, and 7(b) and the effective date for the rest, which adds confusion.

## Structural issues

34. **No severability clause.** If a court strikes Sec. 2(1)(B) or the criminal provision, whether the rest survives is left to default doctrine.

35. **No findings or statement of constitutional authority.** This makes it harder to defend the Act's extraterritorial reach and gives courts no interpretive guidance for the ambiguous terms above.

## Two notes for coverage

- The title says "Prohibition," but the text is threshold-based, grandfathers existing licenses, and sunsets in 10 years. Describing it as a flat "ban" would overstate it.
- These issues cut both ways. Items 1–5 and 12–19 are under-inclusion problems, while items 6–8, 11, 23, 25, and 27 create litigation risk for the bill's defenders.

I haven't seen the pre-amendment text. If you send the original bill, I can compare it against the October 6 manager's amendment to show which problems the amendment introduced or fixed.
